newsitem.title: ITALY: EU ministers gather for Treaty celebrations.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers gather for Treaty celebrations.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers gathered on Tuesday to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome amid renewed worries over foreign policy and the bloc's ambitious plans for a single currency.
The treaty, signed on March 25, 1957, created the European Economic Community, the six-nation common market that has become today's 15-nation European Union.
"For 40 years the European Union has been synonymous with peace and prosperity," Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini wrote in a special programme for the event.

The ministerial meeting was being held in the Campidoglio, Rome's Renaissance city hall where the original six gathered in 1957 to tie their economies so tightly together that they could never again go to war.

Dini stirred the waters early with comments in the Italian business daily Il Sole 24 Ore that Europe would benefit from a 12-month delay to economic and monetary union (EMU), due to start on January 1, 1999.
Arriving for the meeting, Dini told reporters he was not asking for a delay and that Italy and others would do their "utmost" to meet the strict rules for qualifying for the single currency.
"My thought was that if the treaty had provided for an extra year, that would have been helpful," he told Reuters.
The ministers were also to have their celebrations distracted by the chaos in Albania.

Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino was to meet the ministers later in the day to discuss his country's problems and ask for EU humanitarian aid backed by a security force to ensure deliveries do not fall into the hands of lawless gunmen.

The bloc is sharply divided between those wishing to take direct action in Albania, including Italy, Denmark and Greece, and those concerned about being dragged into more Bosnia-style turmoil, notably Britain and Germany.
The ministers were also to discuss the state of the inter-governmental conference (IGC), the bloc's treaty review to finish in June in Amsterdam.

France, Germany, Italy and others were expected to present a sweeping proposal to incorporate the Western European Union (WEU) defence grouping into the EU over a period of time as a way of creating a joint defence policy.
But the plan has been vehemently opposed by defence powerhouse Britain and the bloc's neutrals, notably Sweden and Ireland.
